title: How does the boto hunt in muddy water?
hook: In the Amazon’s murky rivers, eyes don’t help much. Ears do.
summary: The boto uses echolocation: it sends out clicks and listens to the echoes to navigate and find prey in murky rivers.

cardBlocks.text: Amazon rivers are often very murky, and seeing in them is hard. So the boto, the Amazon river dolphin, probably relies much more on echolocation than on sight to find its way and catch prey. It sends out sounds, called clicks, and uses the echoes that come back to "see" what is around it.

The clicks are mostly between 85 and 100 kilohertz, far above what human ears can hear. On its head the boto has a melon, an organ used for biosonar, whose shape it can change with its muscles when echolocating. There is evidence that it uses echolocation both to navigate and to catch prey.
In murky water, the boto finds its way and its prey by the echoes of its own clicks: echolocation.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Unlike ocean dolphins, the boto’s neck vertebrae are not fused, so it can turn its head up to 90 degrees. That helps it manoeuvre in the flooded forest and catch prey.
Despite its small eyes, the boto seems to see well both in and out of the water. It breathes every 30 to 110 seconds.
